name: Faroese
family: Indo-European, Germanic, North Germanic, West Scandinavian (Insular)
variety: Faroese of the central area around Tórshavn, the variety most descriptions take as their base; dialect differences in the stops are noted
sources: Árnason, Kristján (2011). The Phonology of Icelandic and Faroese. Oxford University Press.
Thráinsson, Höskuldur; Petersen, Hjalmar P.; Jacobsen, Jógvan í Lon; Hansen, Zakaris Svabo (2004). Faroese: An Overview and Reference Grammar. Tórshavn: Føroya Fróðskaparfelag.
Lockwood, W. B. (1955). An Introduction to Modern Faroese. Copenhagen: Munksgaard.
Barnes, Michael P. and Weyhe, Eivind (1994). Faroese. In König and van der Auwera (eds.), The Germanic Languages. London: Routledge.
Helgason, Pétur (2002). Preaspiration in the Nordic Languages: Synchronic and Diachronic Aspects. Doctoral dissertation, Stockholm University.
Helgason, Pétur (2003). Faroese preaspiration. In Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Barcelona.
contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated stops and affricates at the start of a word, all voiceless (t in tala against d in dalur, k in koma against g in góður); there are no voiced stops
preaspirated versus plain stops after a vowel (koppur, hattur, takk with preaspiration against the unaspirated stops written bb, dd, gg)

every stressed vowel has a long and a short form, chosen by syllable structure, and the two often differ in quality: a is [ɛaː] long and [a] short, ó is [ɔuː] long and [œ] short, ú is [ʉuː] long and [ʏ] short, í is [ʊiː] long and [ʊi] short, ey is [ɛiː] long and [ɛ] short
eight long diphthongs beside five long monophthongs
palatal affricates /tʃʰ tʃ/ and /ʃ/ versus velar stops and /sk/, in part predictable from the following front vowel
only three vowels [a ɪ ʊ] in unstressed syllables
allophony: pp, tt, kk and p, t, k before l, n are preaspirated after a short vowel (koppur [ˈkʰɔʰpːʊɹ], hattur, vatn [vaʰtn̥]); in the central and northern dialects p, t, k are also preaspirated after long non-close vowels and diphthongs (eta [ˈeːʰta], bátur [ˈpɔaːʰtʊɹ]) but plain after close vowels (vita); in the south the stops after long vowels are plain and unaspirated
sonorants are voiceless before p, t, k, and /l/ is then a voiceless lateral fricative (hjálpa [ˈjɔɬpa], mjólk [mjœɬk], hvalpur, lampa, vanta)
k, g and sk before the front vowels e, i, y, ey and before j are [tʃʰ tʃ ʃ] (kirkja [ˈtʃʰɪɹ̥tʃa], gera [ˈtʃeːɹa], skip [ʃiːp]); tj, kj are [tʃʰ], dj, gj are [tʃ], sj, skj, stj are [ʃ]

written ð and g between vowels are silent, and a glide fills the hiatus: [j] after í, ý, ei, ey, oy and before i, [w] after ú, ó, [v] before u after other vowels (maður [ˈmɛaːvʊɹ], dagur [ˈtɛaːvʊɹ], veður [ˈveːvʊɹ], góður [ˈkɔuːwʊɹ], eiga [ˈaiːja])

skerping: before ggj and gv the vowels are short and changed: ógv is [ɛkv], úgv is [ɪkv], eyggj is [ɛtʃː], íggj and ýggj are [ʊtʃː], eiggj is [atʃː], oyggj is [ɔtʃː] (sjógvur [ˈʃɛkvʊɹ], kúgv [kʰɪkv], oyggj [ɔtʃː], nýggjur [ˈnʊtʃːʊɹ])
ll is [tl] and nn after a diphthong is [tn] (fjall [fjatl], seinni, oynni); rn is [tn] or retroflex [ɳ] (horn, barn)
/r/ is an approximant [ɹ], voiceless before p, t, k; with a following s, t, d, n, l it gives retroflex [ʂ ʈ ɖ ɳ ɭ] (først, stórt)
hv is [kv] (hvussu [ˈkvʊsːʊ]); hj is [j] in most words (hjálpa, hjarta) and [tʃʰ] in some (hjól)

vowels are long in stressed open syllables: at the end of a word, before a single consonant, and before some clusters of a stop plus r or l (eta, vita, akrar); they are short before long consonants and other clusters
unstressed endings have [a ɪ ʊ] (-ar, -ir, -ur); many speakers merge unstressed [ɪ] and [ʊ] in some endings
/v/ is a weak fricative or approximant
phonotactics: a stressed syllable is heavy: long vowel or diphthong, or short vowel plus long consonant or cluster
there are no voiced stops; the two stop series differ by aspiration
unstressed syllables have only [a ɪ ʊ]
hiatus inside words is filled by a glide [j w v]
onset clusters of up to three consonants (str, skr, spj)

stress.rule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable; later members of compounds have secondary stress; some loans and words with certain prefixes stress a later syllable.
stress.cues: duration of the stressed rhyme (long vowel or long consonant), pitch movement when accented, and intensity; unstressed syllables have a reduced set of vowels

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed syllables have only the three short vowels [a ɪ ʊ], which may be centralised or merged
rhythm.notes: Classification by general description; I know of no instrumental rhythm study that I can cite.

length.notes: Vowel length is decided by syllable structure, as in Icelandic; long and short forms of one vowel often differ in quality, so the difference is audible as quality as well as length. Long consonants follow short stressed vowels. I cannot quote duration figures with confidence.

intonation.declarative: accents on stressed syllables, falling nuclear accent and low final boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by verb-first word order; whether the usual tune rises or falls at the end is not settled in the descriptions known to me
intonation.wh_question: accent on or after the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: high or rising end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: peak on or just after the word-initial stressed syllable, followed by a fall
intonation.notes: Low confidence: Faroese intonation has been studied little. Árnason (2011) is the main account.

tone.notes: Faroese has no word accents of the Swedish and Norwegian kind.

phonation: preaspiration of stops after short vowels and, in the central and northern dialects, after long non-close vowels
voiceless sonorants before p, t, k, with a voiceless lateral fricative for /l/
postaspiration of initial /pʰ tʰ kʰ tʃʰ/

problems: stress is wrong in most words: the pronunciation list (about 228,000 entries) writes '%' before the first vowel of nearly every word, eSpeak NG reads '%' as 'unstressed', and no stress rule is set for fo, so the default rule puts the stress on a later syllable (eta is [eːdˈa], koppur [kɔhbːˈʊr], veður [veːvˈʊr]); Faroese has initial stress
the offglide of the diphthongs ei, ey, oy, í is written with the phoneme J, which in the base table is a voiced palatal stop, so eiga, oyra, seinni come out with a stop inside the vowel ([aɟːja])
long diphthongs are written as two vowel phonemes (E plus A:, O plus A:, O plus W:), which count as two syllables; the stress mark can then fall between the two halves (maður, dagur, bátur)
several vowel phonemes of the table (2, 3, 8, 9) have no IPA name and print as digits in the IPA trace, and the phonemes 4 and 5 are declared as vowels but play consonant recordings

words that are not in the list are read by fo_rules, which has about one rule per letter: no vowel length rule, no preaspiration, no palatalisation apart from k and g before i, no skerping, ð always [v], and penultimate stress

the voiceless lateral before p, t, k is written with the dark l of the base table (mjólk, hjálpa), and the long vowels E: and W: have the length value of short vowels, as in the Icelandic table, whose definitions this table repeats
questions are given the generic question tune
good: the list entries encode preaspiration as [h] plus stop (vatn, koppur, hattur, takk)
the list entries encode the hiatus glides (maður, veður with [v], góður with [w]), the palatal affricates (kirkja, gera, kjøt) and the skerping forms (oyggj, nýggjur, sjógvur)
all stops are voiceless and unaspirated after vowels

notes: The consonant list is phonetic. [yː] and [aː] occur in loans. The short diphthongs ʊi, ai, ɔi are the short forms of í, ei, oy. The statements about the eSpeak NG list rest on the phoneme output of the built voice for words such as eta, koppur, maður, eiga; the symbols of the list seem to follow another transcription convention than the one eSpeak NG uses, which would explain the stress marks and the use of J. I give no formant, duration or voice onset time values because I cannot quote published figures with confidence.
